analysis.one_liner: Phase out the manufacture and use of toxic PFAS "forever chemicals" over three years.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban PFAS manufacturing within two years died in a House committee without a floor vote, despite a subcommittee advancing it unanimously in September 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made "forever chemicals" used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, and firefighting foam, and they have been linked to health problems while building up in water and soil. This bill would have forced the EPA to regulate and then largely ban their manufacture: new PFAS banned after six months, all manufacture after two years, and processing or sale after three years. Manufacturers would also have to handle disposal, warn users, and take back unsold chemicals. It never got a vote in the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink contaminated water, live near PFAS manufacturing or disposal sites, or use PFAS-containing products — mainly residents of affected communities.

how_it_helps.text: Bans all new PFAS chemicals six months after enactment and all PFAS manufacture within two years.
Requires EPA rules on safe disposal, clear warning labels, and public reporting of PFAS manufacturing.
Makes manufacturers take back and properly dispose of unprocessed PFAS, and replace or repurchase it at the customer's election.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and companies that use PFAS in products would face the cost of phasing out and safely disposing of these chemicals.

drawbacks.text: The phase-out is fast: two years to stop all PFAS manufacturing, with exemptions capped at one year, could disrupt supply chains for products that rely on PFAS (like some medical devices or electronics) before substitutes are ready.
The bill addresses manufacture and processing but does not by itself fund cleanup of PFAS already in water supplies and soil, which is where much of the public exposure lies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health rationale is strong: PFAS persist in the environment and are linked to serious health risks, so a phase-out protects the public. The trade-off is speed — a two-year ban leaves little room for companies to develop substitutes, and the bill's one-year exemption limit is tight. On balance it is a pro-public bill whose main weakness is abruptness rather than direction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and a subcommittee advanced it by voice vote, but the full committee never acted and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Madeleine Dean introduced the bill on May 8, 2019, with three Democratic cosponsors joining as original sponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment and Consumer Protection subcommittees.
A subcommittee held a hearing in May 2019 and marked it up in September 2019, forwarding it to the full committee by voice vote.
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never reported the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and PFAS-dependent industries, which avoided a mandatory phase-out and continued using and selling PFAS products.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical manufacturers who kept making PFAS

for.name: Rep. Madeleine Dean
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed a phased ban on PFAS manufacturing.

for.name: Mrs. Dingell, Mr. Cisneros, and Mr. Khanna
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors to back the bill at introduction.

for.name: 3 more House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to six members of the House Democratic caucus.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing and marked the bill up, forwarding it to the full committee by voice vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Full committee, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the House floor after its subcommittee advanced it, letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never got a recorded vote, so no roll-call data exists on broader support or opposition.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers (PFAS producers like 3M, Chemours, DuPont)
industries.note: The bill would have banned PFAS manufacturing within two years, ending a major product line. These companies benefit from the bill's failure because they can continue making and selling PFAS.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers using PFAS (e.g., nonstick cookware, outdoor clothing)
industries.note: These companies would have had to reformulate products or seek narrow exemptions. They gain from the bill's failure but face reputational and regulatory risk from PFAS in their goods.
